On the Claude API, Skills run in a sandboxed container with no network access, so the step calling your REST API fails, while Claude Code Skills have full network access (Option A). C is the tempting trap, but the stem says the code execution tool is in the request and the rest of the Skill works, so the container is running. B's lack of syncing affects availability, not a single step, and D is wrong because bundled scripts do run.

stem: Your engineers use Claude Code and an internal app built on the Claude API. You want one custom Skill available to all of them without each person uploading or installing it. Which approaches achieve that?

choices.text: Upload it once in claude.ai settings, where it's shared with the organization
choices.reason: Custom Skills in claude.ai are individual to each user: each team member must upload separately.

choices.text: Upload it through the Claude API, where custom Skills are shared workspace-wide
choices.reason: Correct: custom Skills uploaded through the API are workspace-wide, so all workspace members can access them.

choices.text: Upload it in claude.ai and let it sync to the API and to Claude Code from there
choices.reason: Custom Skills don't sync across surfaces: Skills uploaded to claude.ai must be uploaded separately to the API.

choices.text: Commit it to the repository's `.claude/skills/` directory for Claude Code
choices.reason: Correct: Claude Code Skills can be project-based (`.claude/skills/`), and can also be shared through plugins.

choices.text: Ask a claude.ai admin to distribute it centrally to every member of the org
choices.reason: claude.ai does not support centralized admin management or org-wide distribution of custom Skills.

takeaway: Skill sharing: claude.ai = per user; **API = workspace-wide**; Claude Code = project `.claude/skills/` or a plugin.
explanation: Sharing depends on the **surface**. Custom Skills uploaded through the Claude API are workspace-wide, so everyone using the internal app gets it (B). For Claude Code, committing the Skill to the repository's `.claude/skills/` directory shares it with the project (D). A is the most tempting wrong pick because a single upload in claude.ai sounds organization-wide, but custom Skills there are individual to each user. C fails because Skills don't sync across surfaces, and E because claude.ai has no org-wide distribution for custom Skills.

stem: A teammate found a handy community Skill from an unknown author for processing invoices and wants to add it to your production agent, which can access customer data. What does Anthropic's Skills guidance say to do?

choices.text: Read the SKILL.md description; if it matches the stated purpose, the Skill is safe
choices.reason: A malicious Skill can direct Claude to act in ways that don't match its stated purpose; review SKILL.md, scripts, images and other resources.

choices.text: Audit every bundled file, scripts included, as you would before installing software
choices.reason: Correct: use Skills only from trusted sources; if you must use an unknown one, audit it thoroughly and treat it like installing software.

choices.text: Install it, because Skills only add instructions and can't execute any code
choices.reason: Skills bundle executable scripts, and malicious Skills can invoke tools such as bash commands or code execution in harmful ways.

choices.text: Install it, since every Skill runs in a sandbox that blocks all outgoing network calls
choices.reason: Network access depends on the surface (Claude Code Skills have full network access), and Skills with data access could leak it externally.

takeaway: Treat a Skill like **software**: trusted sources only, and audit every file, scripts included, before production use.
explanation: Treat a Skill like **installing software**. Skills bundle executable scripts and can invoke tools such as bash or code execution, so a Skill from an unknown author must be audited thoroughly, every file included, before it touches customer data (Option B). A is the tempting trap: a matching description proves nothing, because a malicious Skill can act differently from its stated purpose. C wrongly says Skills can't run code, and D wrongly assumes a sandbox, since Claude Code Skills have full network access.

stem: Your Agent SDK support bot should use only your custom MCP tools, never built-ins like Bash or Read. You list your tools in `allowedTools`, yet Claude still sometimes tries Bash. What should you change?

choices.text: Add a scoped `disallowedTools` rule such as `"Bash(rm *)"` to deny risky calls
choices.reason: A scoped rule leaves the tool in context and denies only matching calls, so Claude may still try Bash; removing it needs `tools` or a bare name.

choices.text: List each custom tool in `allowedTools` again, using its full `mcp__` tool name
choices.reason: `allowedTools` works at the permission layer: listed tools skip the prompt, but other tools remain available to Claude.

choices.text: Pass `tools: []` so every built-in is removed and only your MCP tools remain
choices.reason: Correct: `tools` controls availability. `tools: []` removes all built-ins, so Claude can only use your MCP tools.

choices.text: Set `readOnlyHint: true` on the custom tools so Claude prefers them to built-ins
choices.reason: `readOnlyHint` controls whether a tool can run in parallel with other read-only tools; it doesn't hide built-ins.

takeaway: `allowedTools` = skip the prompt; `tools` = what exists. To hide built-ins, use `tools: []` (or bare names in `disallowedTools`).
explanation: `allowedTools` and `tools` work at different layers. `allowedTools` is the permission layer: listed tools skip the prompt, but other tools stay available, which is why Claude still tries Bash. `tools` controls what exists, so `tools: []` removes every built-in and leaves only your MCP tools (Option C). A is the tempting trap because a deny rule sounds strong, but a scoped rule like `Bash(rm *)` keeps the tool in context and denies only matching calls. B repeats the permission-layer fix, and D's `readOnlyHint` doesn't hide built-ins.

stem: You want Claude Code to audit an entire large codebase for security issues, with a second set of agents verifying each finding before you see it. Which feature fits best?

choices.text: A single subagent that reads the whole codebase and returns one summary
choices.reason: Subagents suit quick, focused workers; a job that outgrows a handful of subagents, or needs findings cross-checked, suits a dynamic workflow.

choices.text: A skill holding the audit checklist, run inside your main conversation
choices.reason: A skill's content adds to your main context window; a codebase-wide audit with verified findings is the docs' example of a workflow.

choices.text: A `PostToolUse` hook that checks each file for issues as Claude edits it
choices.reason: Hooks fire at lifecycle events for automation that must run every time; they don't plan an audit or cross-check its findings.

choices.text: A dynamic workflow: a script Claude writes that runs many subagents
choices.reason: Correct: a dynamic workflow runs many subagents in the background and returns one result; the docs' example is an audit with agents verifying each finding.

takeaway: A few focused tasks → **subagents**. Big jobs or cross-checked findings → a **dynamic workflow**.
explanation: The scale and the **cross-checking** are the clues. A dynamic workflow is a script Claude writes that runs many subagents in the background and returns one result, and the docs' own example is an audit with agents verifying each finding (Option D). A is the tempting trap because a subagent isolates heavy reading, but subagents suit quick, focused workers, and a single one can't cross-check its findings. B's skill content adds to your main context, and C's hook fires on edits rather than planning an audit.

stem: In a large TypeScript monorepo, Claude Code reads many files just to find where a symbol is defined or used, which is slow and burns context. What does the Claude Code guide suggest adding?

choices.text: A code intelligence plugin for TypeScript, which connects a language server
choices.reason: Correct: code intelligence gives symbol-level navigation and type errors; symbol lookups often replace broad file reads, so context use can go down.

choices.text: A subagent that greps the whole repository and reports where each symbol lives
choices.reason: A subagent isolates the reads from your context, but still reads the files; the guide's trigger here is a code intelligence plugin.

choices.text: A CLAUDE.md section that lists where each of the main symbols is defined
choices.reason: CLAUDE.md loads in full every session; for symbol hunting the guide points to a code intelligence plugin instead.

choices.text: A hook that indexes every file after each edit and prints the whole index
choices.reason: Hook output lands in context, so printing a full index adds context rather than saving it.

takeaway: Claude hunting for definitions? Install a **code intelligence plugin**: language-server lookups replace broad file reads.
explanation: The problem is broad file reads used just to **find symbols**. A code intelligence plugin connects a language server, giving symbol-level navigation and type errors, and symbol lookups often replace broad file reads, so context use can go down (Option A). B is the tempting trap because a subagent keeps the reads out of your context, but it still reads the files. C's CLAUDE.md section loads in full every session, and D's printed index lands in context, adding to it rather than saving it.

stem: You're moving your team's practices into Claude Code extensions. Which of these belong in hooks rather than skills?

choices.text: Blocking any edit to `.env` files, with no exceptions
choices.reason: Correct: a rule that must hold every time belongs in a hook; a `PreToolUse` hook that blocks the edit is enforcement, not a request.

choices.text: A `/release` checklist that Claude adapts to each release
choices.reason: A checklist Claude decides how to apply is the docs' own example of a skill: a `/release` checklist.

choices.text: Your API style guide, for Claude to consult while coding
choices.reason: Reference material such as an API style guide is knowledge rather than a script, so it belongs in a skill.

choices.text: A debugging playbook Claude applies to each new bug
choices.reason: A debugging playbook needs Claude to decide how to apply the steps, which makes it a skill, not a hook.

choices.text: Posting a Slack message whenever a session ends
choices.reason: Correct: an action that should happen the same way every time without Claude thinking, like posting to Slack when a session ends, is a hook.

takeaway: **Hook** = fires every time, no judgment (block, lint, notify). **Skill** = knowledge or steps Claude applies with judgment.
explanation: The dividing line is **judgment**. A hook fires every time with no thinking, so it fits a rule that must always hold, like blocking any edit to `.env` (A), and a fixed action like posting to Slack when a session ends (E). B is the most tempting wrong pick because a release checklist sounds procedural, but Claude adapts it to each release, and the docs use `/release` as a skill example. The style guide (C) is reference knowledge, and the debugging playbook (D) needs Claude to decide how to apply it, so both are skills.

stem: Your invoice Skill describes how to validate a form, and Claude writes fresh validation code from those instructions on every run. Results vary and token use is high. What does the Agent Skills overview suggest?

choices.text: Paste the full validation code into SKILL.md so Claude can copy it on every run
choices.reason: The SKILL.md body enters context when the Skill triggers; a bundled script's code never does, and running it is more reliable.

choices.text: Move the validation steps into the Skill's `description` so they're always in context
choices.reason: The description is Level 1 metadata (~100 tokens per Skill) that Claude matches to decide when to trigger; it isn't where procedures go.

choices.text: Bundle a `validate.py` script that Claude runs, so only its output enters context
choices.reason: Correct: scripts give deterministic operations, and only their output uses tokens, making them far more efficient than generating equivalent code.

choices.text: Split the steps into several smaller Skills, each with its own trigger description
choices.reason: More Skills still leave Claude generating the code each time; bundled scripts are how a Skill gets reliable, low-token operations.

takeaway: Deterministic step in a Skill? Ship it as a **script**: Claude runs it, and only the output costs tokens.
explanation: When a Skill step is **deterministic**, ship it as a script. A bundled `validate.py` that Claude runs gives consistent results, and only its output uses tokens, which is far more efficient than generating equivalent code each run (Option C). A is the tempting trap because pasted code seems reusable, but the SKILL.md body enters context when the Skill triggers, while a bundled script's code never does. B misuses the description, which is trigger metadata, and D still leaves Claude generating code every time.
